summary: A classification topic for ages 7-9: extend the child's map of the solar system beyond the eight planets to smaller bodies and pin down three commonly-confused categories. Asteroids are rocky bodies mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter; comets are icy 'dirty snowballs' that grow a glowing tail only when near the Sun (ice vaporises); and meteoroid→meteor→meteorite is ONE rock named by WHERE it is (a rock in space, the glowing streak of light as it burns in the atmosphere, and the landed rock). The two load-bearing moves are rocky-vs-icy (asteroid vs comet) and location-defines-the-name (meteor trio). A counter-intuitive fact to surface: a comet's tail is pushed by sunlight and the solar wind, so it always points AWAY from the Sun, not trailing behind the comet's motion.
misconceptions: Thinking a comet's tail streams out BEHIND it like exhaust or a scarf, rather than always pointing away from the Sun.
Believing comets are burning / on fire — they are icy; the tail is vaporising ice and dust lit by sunlight, not flames.
Using meteoroid, meteor and meteorite interchangeably, not realising they are the same object named by location (space / atmosphere / ground).
Calling a meteor a 'shooting star' and thinking it really is a star.
Assuming asteroids are scattered everywhere or are tiny planets, rather than mostly rocky bodies concentrated in the belt.
Confusing asteroids and comets — not grasping rocky-vs-icy as the key difference.

activities.title: Explore the solar-system map: tap and reveal the small bodies
steps: Start from a single wide solar-system scene the child already recognises: Sun, inner planets, and the asteroid belt drawn as a ring of rubble between Mars and Jupiter, plus a comet on a looping path and a meteor streaking into Earth's sky.
Tap the rubble-ring between Mars and Jupiter so it lights up and is labelled: 'asteroids — space rocks, mostly in the belt between Mars and Jupiter.'
Tap the bright comet and zoom into its icy nucleus, fuzzy coma, and streaming tail; read that a comet is an icy 'dirty snowball' that grows a tail only when it nears the Sun.
Lift a flap asking 'which way does the tail point?' and discover it points AWAY from the Sun, not behind the comet like a scarf or exhaust.

Tap the 'shooting star' streak and follow one glowing arc that splits into three labelled stages: meteoroid (a rock in space) → meteor (the glowing streak of light made as the rock burns in the sky) → meteorite (any piece of the rock that survives and lands on the ground; most burn up completely).

Lift a final flap on the 'shooting star' to reveal it is not a star at all: the bright streak is the light made when a tiny space rock burns up in our air — the rock itself is the meteoroid, and the glowing streak is the meteor.
activities.insight: Asteroids are rocky and live in the belt; comets are icy and grow a tail (which points away from the Sun) only near the Sun; and meteoroid/meteor/meteorite name the SAME rock by where it is — a rock in space (meteoroid), the streak of light it makes while burning up (meteor), and the landed rock (meteorite), so a 'shooting star' is a light-streak, not a star.

activities.title: Drag the comet round its orbit and watch the tail swing
steps: Drag a comet along an elliptical orbit around the Sun.
As the comet approaches the Sun, watch the tail lengthen and bloom; as it moves away again, watch it shrink.

Pay attention to the tail's direction as the comet rounds the Sun: watch it continuously re-orient to point away from the Sun, so that on the outbound leg the tail actually LEADS the comet rather than trailing it.
Predict, before dragging, which way the tail will point when the comet is heading back out, then check.
activities.insight: A comet's tail is pushed away from the Sun by sunlight and the solar wind, so it always points away from the Sun regardless of which way the comet is travelling — and it grows only when the comet is near enough for its ices to warm and stream off.

activities.title: Sort and sequence the small bodies
steps: Sort a set of objects into three bins: rocky asteroid (belt), icy comet (tail near the Sun), and meteor-journey.
Put the meteoroid→meteor→meteorite stages in order and label each by its location (space / atmosphere / ground).
Answer: which way does a comet's tail point, and where in the solar system do most asteroids orbit?
Explain in your own words why a comet grows a tail only when it comes close to the Sun.
activities.insight: Secure recall and discrimination of the three categories and the naming-by-location rule for the meteor trio, including the surprising tail direction.

checkQuestion: A comet is racing through space and grows a long glowing tail. Does the tail always trail out BEHIND the comet, in the direction it came from — like smoke behind a rocket? Or does it point some other way? Tell me WHY.
checkAnswer: The tail does NOT simply trail behind the comet's motion. A comet's tail always points AWAY FROM THE SUN, whichever way the comet happens to be travelling, because sunlight and the solar wind push the comet's gas and dust away from the Sun. So as a comet rounds the Sun and heads back out, its tail actually goes ahead of it — still pointing away from the Sun. (A comet is an icy body that only grows a tail when it nears the Sun and its ices warm and stream off.)
